title: Adaptive admission signal controller for high-QPS batching and KV memory pressure
creator: Maya Chen
description: When serving sustained high QPS bursts (1k-5k req/s), we observe cascading latency and tail spikes caused by aggressive batching windows plus KV cache growth that exhausts GPU memory. This ticket implements an adaptive admission-signal controller that harmonizes batching thresholds with live KV memory pressure and GPU headroom estimates so we maintain p99 latency SLAs while maximizing throughput and avoiding OOMs.
background: Current runtime uses a fixed micro-batching window and a simple 'reject-if-mem-near-capacity' heuristic. During large sustained spikes we saw: p95 latency jump from ~180ms to >1200ms, GPU memory usage climb leading to KV slab fragmentation and eviction storms, and several customer incidents where fallbacks to cheaper models were late. Existing tickets improved smoothing/hysteresis but did not consider joint signals from KV slab state and batch admission rate simultaneously.
proposed_solution: Introduce an Admission Signal Controller (ASC) with three coordinated components: 1) Ingress EWMA and surge detector to adapt batching window and max-batch-size in soft steps, 2) GPU headroom estimator combining free VRAM, live KV slab fragmentation ratio and active KV item count to produce a continuous headroom score, 3) Graceful backpressure policy: soft throttles (reduce batching wait time, lower max-concurrent-batches) that run proactively; hard actions (route to overflow capacity, 429 with Retry-After, or degrade to lightweight model variant) only when headroom < 8% or fragmentation > 0.45. ASC exposes metrics and admission-hint headers to downstream proxies for observability. We also add a prioritized KV compaction job triggered when headroom > 20% to reclaim slab fragmentation in background.
experiments: lab-2026-02-12: Synthetic 3k RPS text-gen workload against replica set (4xA100-like). Baseline (fixed window): p95=1180ms, p99=2200ms, OOMs=1 per hour.

trial-asc-v1-2026-02-18: ASC with EWMA alpha=0.2, soft-thresholds: reduce wait by 40% on surge, hard threshold headroom 6%. Results: p95=430ms, p99=810ms, no OOMs in 6h run, throughput sustained at 2.9k RPS average.
trial-asc-v2-2026-02-22: Added KV compaction trigger and prioritization of hot prefixes. Results: 10% lower average token cost, 12% fewer eviction cycles, p99 improved to 720ms under same load.

canary-0.5%-2026-02-26: Canary test in prod region us-west1. Observed slight increase in small latency tails for short-lived requests due to conservative hard caps; adjusted rollback window and Retry-After semantics.
notes: all experiment logs and perf dashboards linked in docs below.
decisions: Use EWMA-based ingress smoothing rather than fixed rate-limit bucket to be responsive to ramp-ups without oscillation.
Expose admission-hint header (x-rw-admission-hint) for optional downstream routing/observability.
Implement soft thresholds by shrinking batching window and lowering max-batch-size before triggering model fallback or 429s.
KV compaction will be background low-priority work that can be preempted when headroom drops below 12%.
Default hard headroom action is to route to overflow pool if available; otherwise return 429 with Retry-After tuned to EWMA estimate.
tradeoffs: Aggressive soft throttling reduces per-request latency but can reduce steady-state throughput for latency-tolerant workloads.
Background KV compaction uses cycles that could otherwise be used for inference — we limit it to idle GPU cycles or dedicated maintenance windows.
Adding admission headers increases surface area for downstream components and requires updates to proxy/router code to make use of hints.
Headroom estimator relies on heuristics (fragmentation ratio, hot item count); misestimation could be conservative and underutilize capacity initially.
